questions.q: What does it mean that LightGBM grows trees leaf-wise?
options: It grows every node at one depth before going deeper
It uses only one leaf per tree
It always splits the leaf that would reduce the loss the most, producing lopsided trees
It removes leaves after training
questions.explain: Leaf-wise growth picks the best leaf to split next, which is why num_leaves is a key complexity control.

questions.q: Which LightGBM setting is the main complexity control, especially on small datasets?
options: num_leaves
verbose
random_state
eval_metric
questions.explain: Leaf-wise trees with many leaves overfit quickly, so num_leaves is the key knob to keep small on small data.

It can handle categorical columns natively via cat_features
It only works with images
It replaces boosting with a single deep tree
questions.explain: CatBoost converts categorical columns using target statistics computed with an ordered scheme, so you name them in cat_features instead of encoding them.

questions.q: In the lesson, the three libraries scored 0.828, 0.830 and 0.831 on one split. What did the five-split repetition show?
options: XGBoost was always clearly worst
CatBoost was always clearly best
The means were 0.836, 0.835 and 0.835 with a split-to-split spread of about 0.006, so the libraries were effectively tied
Repeating splits is invalid for boosted models
questions.explain: The differences between libraries were much smaller than the variation between splits, so accuracy alone does not separate them here.

questions.q: A dataset has several categorical columns with hundreds of levels each. Which library is a sensible first thing to try?
options: None of them can use categorical data
XGBoost, after one-hot encoding every level by hand
LightGBM with num_leaves set as high as possible
CatBoost, with those columns passed in cat_features
questions.explain: CatBoost's native categorical handling avoids the column explosion of one-hot encoding high-cardinality features.
